text.p: The following are the main stories from Thursday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Tax talks break down in under an hour amid mutual recriminations. Now everything takes usual legislative procedure
- Bonn opposition demands tougher controls on refuse disposal

- There is no lack of work, just not enough viable jobs, according to Germany's association of self-employed. Group demanded competitiveness and lack of price restrictions on the jobs market in a pamphlet
- HBV white collar workers union argues that longer shop opening hours has not led to increase in sales
- Social benefits for Bosnian civil war refugees drop. Germany's 16 states who have taken in over 300,000 refugees are urged to use the money saved in building homes in Bosnia
HANDELSBLATT

- Bonn plans reform shaped by coalition only. Tax talks between Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition and the opposition Social Democrats break down amid mutual recriminations. Coalition considers trying to push through the legislation in one chunk in 1999.
- Siemens disappoints stock market traders with worse than expected results
- Sales down despite longer opening hours, HBV white-collar workers union say
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG

- Search for tax compromise fails as talks in Chancellery between Chancellor Kohl's coalition and opposition Social Democrats break down. Government and SPD blame each other for politics that are blocking reforms
- German lower house rehabilitates Wehrmacht deserters
- Employees did not call in sick at work so often in first quarter 1997, according to the Health Ministry
- Association of small to medium-sized firms reject plans for introduction of single European currency, the euro
DIE WELT
- Attempts to reach tax consensus fails. Bonn coalition and opposition Social Democrats part without result amid mutual recriminations. Issue will be decided now in mediation committee
- Less social benefits planned for asylum seekers
- German Wehrmacht (World War Two) army deserters are rehabilitated
- DGB German trade union federation members demonstrate in Duesseldorf to keep jobs
